scenes.head: The statement of cash flows
scenes.sub: Prepare a full year’s statement of cash flows: decide what counts as cash, classify every receipt and payment under US GAAP and IFRS, work out the direct-method lines from the accrual records, and disclose what changed without any cash moving.

segs.say: The statement of cash flows. Prepare a full year’s statement of cash flows: decide what counts as cash, classify every receipt and payment under US GAAP and IFRS, work out the direct-method lines from the accrual records, and disclose what changed without any cash moving.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Explain what the statement of cash flows reports, and decide which items are cash and cash equivalents.
Classify receipts and payments as operating, investing or financing under US GAAP (ASC 230), and state how IAS 7 differs before and after the IFRS 18 amendments.
Calculate direct-method operating cash flows from income statement figures and the changes in the related balance sheet accounts.
Prepare a statement of cash flows by the direct method, with a disclosure of noncash investing and financing activities.
Explain why ASC 230 encourages the direct method although most companies use the indirect method.

scenes.head: Lantern’s first financial year ends on 31 December 2026.

segs.say: Lantern’s first financial year ends on 31 December 2026. The business opened on 1 March with no cash at all and closes the year with $42,940 in the bank, after net income of $27,387. Coastline Bank asks for the year’s statements for its loan file, and the loan officer has two questions the income statement can’t answer: where did the $42,940 come from, and can Lantern carry the $20,000 note it signed for the van, whose first $5,000 instalment is due on 1 June 2027?

scenes.head: The income statement measures performance on the accrual basis, and the balance sheet shows positions at one date.

segs.say: The income statement measures performance on the accrual basis, and the balance sheet shows positions at one date. Neither shows how cash moved. The statement of cash flows explains the change in cash and cash equivalents during the period by listing the cash received and paid, grouped as operating activities, investing activities and financing activities. Under US GAAP its rules are in the FASB’s Accounting Standards Codification, Topic 230 (ASC 230); under IFRS they are in IAS 7. Both are titled Statement of Cash Flows.

scenes.head: Readers use the statement to judge what the other statements hide: whether a business generates cash from its operations or depends on owners and…

segs.say: Readers use the statement to judge what the other statements hide: whether a business generates cash from its operations or depends on owners and lenders, how much it spends on long-term assets, whether it can pay its debts and dividends from its own cash, and why net income and cash differ. A lender cares most about the first and the third; an owner deciding on a dividend cares about all four.

scenes.head: In F01 you prepared a statement of cash flows for Lantern’s first month by listing each cash transaction.

segs.say: In F01 you prepared a statement of cash flows for Lantern’s first month by listing each cash transaction. A year is different in three ways: there are thousands of transactions, so the accountant works from summaries and from the accrual records rather than from each bank entry; every kind of timing difference appears at once, from receivables, inventory and payables to customer deposits, prepaid insurance, accrued interest and income taxes; and the classification rules matter more, because the two frameworks disagree about interest and dividends. This lesson covers the statement as a whole and the direct method; the next lesson covers the indirect method, which reaches the same operating total by starting from net income.
From no cash to $42,940: Lantern’s first year by activity (fictional figures in dollars).

scenes.head: One line of the balance sheet

segs.say: One line of the balance sheet. The statement explains a single balance sheet figure: cash and cash equivalents, $0 at 1 March and $42,940 at 31 December for Lantern. Every entry that changes that figure appears in the statement, and every entry that doesn’t stays out, even the $20,000 note Lantern signed for its van. Investing and financing transactions without cash are disclosed beside the statement instead.

scenes.head: Cash means currency and deposits that can be withdrawn on demand.

segs.say: Cash means currency and deposits that can be withdrawn on demand. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible to known amounts of cash and so near their maturity that changes in interest rates can hardly affect their value. The ASC 230 glossary adds that generally only investments with original maturities of three months or less qualify, where “original” means from the date the business acquired the investment. So a three-year Treasury note bought three months before it matures qualifies, but a note the business has held for years does not become a cash equivalent as its maturity approaches. Treasury bills, commercial paper and money market funds are the usual examples (ASC 230-10-20).

scenes.head: IAS 7 uses almost the same definition and says an investment normally qualifies only when it has a short maturity of, say, three months or less from…

segs.say: IAS 7 uses almost the same definition and says an investment normally qualifies only when it has a short maturity of, say, three months or less from the date of acquisition; equity investments are excluded unless they are cash equivalents in substance, such as preferred shares bought shortly before a set redemption date (IAS 7, paragraphs 6–7). Because cash and cash equivalents are treated as one pool, moving money between them is not a cash flow: buying a 60-day Treasury bill with cash changes neither the total nor any activity, and ASC 230-10-45-5 treats such purchases and sales as cash management whose details need not be reported. A nine-month certificate of deposit is different: it is usually reported as a short-term investment, and buying it is an investing outflow.

scenes.head: Each business must disclose its policy for deciding which items are cash equivalents (ASC 230-10-50-1), and a US GAAP statement explains the change…

segs.say: Each business must disclose its policy for deciding which items are cash equivalents (ASC 230-10-50-1), and a US GAAP statement explains the change in the total of cash, cash equivalents and any restricted cash (ASC 230-10-45-4). Bank overdrafts are a difference between the frameworks: US GAAP never includes them in cash, whereas under IAS 7 an overdraft that is repayable on demand and forms an integral part of cash management is included (paragraph 8). Lantern holds no cash equivalents, so its cash is the balance of its business bank account.

chapters.title: Classifying cash flows under US GAAP

scenes.head: ASC 230 defines investing and financing activities and makes operating activities the remainder.

segs.say: ASC 230 defines investing and financing activities and makes operating activities the remainder. Investing covers acquiring and disposing of long-term productive assets and investments, and making and collecting loans. Financing covers dealings with owners and creditors as providers of capital: issuing stock, borrowing, repaying amounts borrowed and paying owners a return. Every receipt and payment that is neither is operating; in practice these are the cash effects of the transactions that make up net income. The table gives the paragraphs that decide the common cases.
Common cash flows under US GAAP

scenes.head: Proceeds from selling equipment or other long-term assets, and collections of loans made to others, are investing inflows.

segs.say: Proceeds from selling equipment or other long-term assets, and collections of loans made to others, are investing inflows. Two rows surprise most students. Interest paid is operating although the loan itself is financing: interest is an expense in net income, and ASC 230 keeps the cash effects of net income together, so only the repayment of principal is financing. Dividends paid are financing although dividends received are operating, for the same reason seen from the other side: a dividend paid distributes profit to owners and is not an expense, while a dividend received is income. Customer deposits are operating receipts even though the revenue isn’t earned yet, because they are cash from customers for goods or services.

scenes.head: Paying for an asset over time needs care.

segs.say: Paying for an asset over time needs care. Only the down payment and amounts paid at the purchase, or soon before or after it, are investing outflows; if the buyer instead takes on debt directly to the seller, that is a financing transaction, and its later principal payments are financing outflows (ASC 230-10-45-13(c)). Lantern paid $4,000 for its espresso equipment on 3 March and the other $8,000 on 2 April, on the supplier’s ordinary 30-day terms: trade credit paid soon after the purchase, not financing, so all $12,000 is an investing outflow for the year. F01’s March statement disclosed the $8,000 as a noncash item only because it was still unpaid at 31 March.

scenes.head: The van was different.

segs.say: The van was different. Lantern paid $10,000 in cash, an investing outflow, and signed a $20,000 note with the dealer’s finance company. The note brought in no cash, so it is not in the statement at all; the principal Lantern repays from 2027 will be a financing outflow and the interest an operating one.

chapters.title: Lantern’s year by the direct method

scenes.head: The statement below is Lantern’s first annual statement of cash flows, built from the cash lines of the year’s entries.

segs.say: The statement below is Lantern’s first annual statement of cash flows, built from the cash lines of the year’s entries. Its operating section uses the direct method: it lists operating receipts and payments by type, as F01’s March statement did.
Lantern Coffee Co., Statement of cash flows (direct method) for the ten months ended 31 December 2026

scenes.head: Cash received from customers of $191,220 combines catering deposits ($4,040) and collections ($51,720), workshop fees ($22,500) and the online shop’s…

segs.say: Cash received from customers of $191,220 combines catering deposits ($4,040) and collections ($51,720), workshop fees ($22,500) and the online shop’s card receipts ($113,985), less refunds paid back to customers’ cards ($1,025). Cash paid to suppliers of $103,330 covers the beans from Kilnworth Roasting, catering supplies, rent, utilities, advertising, insurance, shipping, fuel, card fees and small costs; employees were paid $41,500, interest $450 and estimated income tax $6,000. Investing shows the equipment and the van’s down payment, and financing shows Ana’s $20,000, Coastline’s $10,000 and the two dividends of $300 and $4,700. The closing figure, $42,940, is the cash on the balance sheet at 31 December.

chapters.title: From the accrual records to the direct-method lines

scenes.head: Few businesses code every bank payment by type as it happens, so preparers usually derive the direct-method lines from the income statement and the…

segs.say: Few businesses code every bank payment by type as it happens, so preparers usually derive the direct-method lines from the income statement and the balance sheet. The logic is the same for every line: start from the accrual amount and adjust it by the change in the balance sheet account that sits between the accrual and the cash. Revenue becomes cash collected after removing the increase in receivables (sold, not yet collected) and the receivables written off (sold, never collected), and adding the increase in unearned revenue (collected, not yet earned). An expense becomes cash paid after adding the increase in a related asset such as inventory or a prepayment (paid for, not yet an expense) and removing the increase in a related liability such as payables (an expense, not yet paid).
Lantern: from the income statement to the direct-method lines
Customers: net revenue of $193,320, less the increase in receivables ($7,380) and the receivable written off ($820), plus the increase in unearned revenue ($6,100).

Suppliers: cost of goods sold, supplies used and the other cash expenses ($105,800), plus the increases in inventory ($5,800), supplies ($640) and prepaid insurance ($300), less the increase in accounts payable ($9,210).
Employees: event wages in cost of services and wages expense ($43,600), less the increase in wages payable ($2,100).
Interest and income taxes: each expense less the increase in the related payable ($750 and $3,129).

scenes.head: Two expenses never reach the direct method: depreciation of $4,800 and bad debt expense of $1,404 used no cash.

segs.say: Two expenses never reach the direct method: depreciation of $4,800 and bad debt expense of $1,404 used no cash. The $820 receivable written off appears instead, in the customers line, because it is a sale that will never be collected. Lantern’s opening balances were all zero, so each change equals the ending balance; in any later year you would use the difference between the opening and closing balances.

scenes.head: One payables account, several suppliers

segs.say: One payables account, several suppliers. Lantern’s $9,210 of accounts payable is $8,400 owed to Kilnworth for beans, $520 to supply vendors and the $290 December utility bill. Because Lantern reports a single “cash paid to suppliers” line, the whole increase goes against that line. A business that reports cash paid for inventory separately must split its payables the same way, or one line will be overstated and another understated.

scenes.head: Some investing and financing transactions involve no cash, or only part of it.

segs.say: Some investing and financing transactions involve no cash, or only part of it. They are left out of the statement, but because they change the business’s assets and liabilities they must be disclosed, either on the same page or in a note the statement refers to (ASC 230-10-50-3 to 50-6; IAS 7, paragraph 43, has the same rule). When a transaction is part cash and part noncash, only the cash part goes in the statement (ASC 230-10-50-5). Converting debt into stock is the classic example (ASC 230-10-50-4); in small businesses the commonest is buying an asset by signing a note.

scenes.head: Lantern’s van is a part-cash purchase: the $10,000 paid is an investing outflow, and the disclosure beneath the statement relates the cash and…

segs.say: Lantern’s van is a part-cash purchase: the $10,000 paid is an investing outflow, and the disclosure beneath the statement relates the cash and noncash parts, as ASC 230-10-50-3 requires: “Van costing $30,000 acquired for $10,000 in cash (shown in investing activities) and $20,000 through a note payable.” A reader who saw only the $10,000 would underestimate both what Lantern invested and what it owes; the disclosure closes that gap. Moving the $5,000 instalment due on 1 June 2027 into current liabilities (adjustment e8) is not a noncash investing or financing activity at all, because no transaction with anyone took place.

chapters.title: Interest, dividends and income taxes under IFRS

scenes.head: IAS 7 agrees with ASC 230 on the three activities but, until the IFRS 18 amendments, gives companies choices that US GAAP does not.

segs.say: IAS 7 agrees with ASC 230 on the three activities but, until the IFRS 18 amendments, gives companies choices that US GAAP does not. A company may classify interest paid as operating or financing, interest and dividends received as operating or investing, and dividends paid as financing or operating, provided it applies its choice consistently from period to period (IAS 7, paragraphs 31, 33 and 34). Taxes on income are operating unless they can be specifically identified with investing or financing activities (paragraph 35).

scenes.head: IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements amends IAS 7 to remove those choices, with effect from the same date as IFRS 18 itself…

segs.say: IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements amends IAS 7 to remove those choices, with effect from the same date as IFRS 18 itself: annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027. A company whose main business is not investing in assets or providing finance to customers must classify interest paid as financing and interest and dividends received as investing (new paragraph 34A), and every company must classify dividends paid as financing (paragraph 33A). Banks, investment companies and others with those main business activities classify interest paid and interest and dividends received to match where the related expense and income appear in their income statement (paragraph 34B). The amendments also make operating profit, rather than profit, the starting point of the indirect method.
Interest and dividends in the statement of cash flows

scenes.head: Which rules apply to Lantern?

segs.say: Which rules apply to Lantern?. Lantern is a US private company reporting under US GAAP, so its $450 of interest paid stays in operating activities and its $5,000 of dividends in financing, whatever IFRS does. The difference matters when you compare it with a company reporting under IFRS: from 2027 that company’s operating cash flow excludes its interest paid and its interest and dividends received, so the two operating figures are not directly comparable until you move those items back.

chapters.title: Direct or indirect: what the standards say and what companies do

scenes.head: ASC 230-10-45-25 encourages the direct method and lists the minimum classes of operating receipts and payments that a company using it must show…

segs.say: ASC 230-10-45-25 encourages the direct method and lists the minimum classes of operating receipts and payments that a company using it must show separately: cash collected from customers; interest and dividends received; other operating receipts; cash paid to employees and other suppliers of goods or services; interest paid; income taxes paid; and other operating payments. IAS 7 also encourages the direct method (paragraph 19). Lantern’s statement shows the classes it has, with suppliers and employees on separate lines.

scenes.head: The encouragement has had little effect: most companies use the indirect method.

segs.say: The encouragement has had little effect: most companies use the indirect method. Three reasons explain the gap. First, US GAAP asks a company that uses the direct method to provide the reconciliation of net income to operating cash flow as well, in a separate schedule (ASC 230-10-45-30), so the direct method means preparing both; IAS 7 asks for the reconciliation only from companies that use the indirect method. Second, accounting systems record revenue and expenses rather than receipts and payments by type, so the direct-method lines must be derived, as you did above, which is laborious in a large organisation. Third, users are familiar with the indirect format, and its starting point ties the statement to the income statement and the balance sheet.

scenes.head: The case for the direct method is plain from Lantern’s statement: a reader sees how much cash came in from customers and went out to suppliers and…

segs.say: The case for the direct method is plain from Lantern’s statement: a reader sees how much cash came in from customers and went out to suppliers and staff, figures that are useful for forecasting and that the indirect method never shows. This course teaches both, because Lantern’s accountant presents the direct method and must still provide the reconciliation, which is the subject of the next lesson.

scenes.head: Opening cash to closing cash

segs.say: Opening cash to closing cash: Cash_(end) = Cash_(beg) + CFO + CFI + CFF.
Cash_(beg), Cash_(end): Cash and cash equivalents at the start and the end of the period ($).
CFO: Net cash from operating activities ($).
CFI: Net cash from investing activities (negative when cash is used) ($).
CFF: Net cash from financing activities (negative when cash is used) ($).
It assumes this: Noncash investing and financing activities are left out; they are disclosed separately.

scenes.head: Cash received from customers

segs.say: Cash received from customers: Cash collected = Revenue − ΔReceivables − Write-offs + ΔUnearned revenue.
Revenue: Net revenue on the income statement (after returns and discounts) ($).
ΔReceivables: Closing minus opening accounts receivable, before the allowance ($).
Write-offs: Receivables written off during the period as uncollectible ($).
ΔUnearned revenue: Closing minus opening unearned revenue (customer deposits and prepayments) ($).
A decrease is a negative Δ, so a fall in receivables adds to the cash collected. Lantern: 193,320 − 7,380 − 820 + 6,100 = 191,220.

scenes.head: Cash paid for inventory

segs.say: Cash paid for inventory: Cash paid = COGS + ΔInventory − ΔPayables.
COGS: Cost of goods sold for the period ($).
ΔInventory: Closing minus opening inventory ($).
ΔPayables: Closing minus opening accounts payable to inventory suppliers ($).
It assumes this: All inventory is bought on account from the suppliers whose payables are used.
COGS + ΔInventory is the period’s purchases. Lantern’s beans: 52,800 + 5,800 − 8,400 = 50,200.

scenes.head: Cash paid for an operating expense

segs.say: Cash paid for an operating expense: Cash paid = Expense + ΔPrepaid − ΔAccrued liability.
Expense: The expense on the income statement (wages, insurance, interest, income tax …) ($).
ΔPrepaid: Closing minus opening prepayment for that expense, if any ($).
ΔAccrued liability: Closing minus opening payable for that expense (wages payable, interest payable …) ($).
Lantern’s interest: 1,200 + 0 − 750 = 450. Depreciation and bad debt expense have no cash payment and are left out.

scenes.head: A clinic’s year, classified

segs.say: Merrow Veterinary Clinic, a fictional business reporting under US GAAP, starts 2026 with $124,000 of cash and cash equivalents. Its cash records for the year show: received from pet owners and insurers $486,000; interest received on a savings account $1,200; paid suppliers of drugs and supplies $142,000; paid employees $238,000; paid rent $36,000; paid interest on its bank loan $4,800; paid income taxes $14,500; bought an X-ray machine for $58,000; sold an old ultrasound scanner for $3,500; bought a 60-day Treasury bill for $20,000 in December, still held at 31 December; put $15,000 into a nine-month certificate of deposit; repaid $24,000 of the loan’s principal; paid dividends of $30,000. It also acquired a $12,000 surgical table by signing a note with the manufacturer. Prepare the statement of cash flows.

scenes.head: A clinic’s year, classified

segs.say: Step 1. Operating (ASC 230-10-45-16 and 45-17, with interest received and paid both operating): 486,000 + 1,200 − 142,000 − 238,000 − 36,000 − 4,800 − 14,500 = 51,900.

Step 2. Investing: the X-ray machine and the certificate of deposit are outflows, the scanner’s sale an inflow: −58,000 + 3,500 − 15,000 = −69,500. The Treasury bill is a cash equivalent (60 days when bought), so buying it moved money inside the cash pool: it is not a cash flow.
Step 3. Financing: −24,000 − 30,000 = −54,000. The surgical table moved no cash: it is a noncash investing and financing activity, disclosed in a note.
Step 4. Net change 51,900 − 69,500 − 54,000 = −71,600; closing cash and cash equivalents 124,000 − 71,600 = 52,400, of which $20,000 is the Treasury bill.

scenes.head: A clinic’s year, classified

segs.say: Operating $51,900; investing ($69,500); financing ($54,000); net decrease $71,600; closing cash and cash equivalents $52,400. The surgical table is disclosed, not included.

Operations produced $51,900, but the clinic spent more than that on equipment and a deposit, and more again on its lender and owners, so cash fell by more than half. The Treasury bill is still part of the $52,400: the clinic didn’t spend that money, it parked it.

chapters.title: Example: The direct method from two balance sheets

scenes.head: The direct method from two balance sheets

segs.say: Coldharbour Tile Supply, a fictional wholesaler, reports for 2027: sales $920,000; cost of goods sold $610,000; wages $142,000; rent $48,000; insurance $6,000; depreciation $21,000; interest $9,000; income tax $21,000; net income $63,000. All its accounts payable are owed to tile suppliers, and its customers pay deposits on special orders. Derive the operating section by the direct method from the balances in the table, and check it against net income.

scenes.head: The direct method from two balance sheets

segs.say: Step 1. Customers: receivables rose, so not all sales were collected; deposits fell, so some revenue was earned from cash received last year: 920,000 − 15,000 − 3,000 = 902,000.
Step 2. Suppliers of tiles: purchases are 610,000 + 12,000 = 622,000; payables fell by 5,000, so Coldharbour paid more than it bought: 622,000 + 5,000 = 627,000.

Step 3. Employees 142,000 − 1,500 = 140,500; rent and insurance 48,000 + 6,000 + 600 = 54,600 (the prepayment grew); interest 9,000 + 500 = 9,500 (the payable fell); income taxes 21,000 − 2,000 = 19,000. Depreciation is left out: it used no cash.

Step 5. Check from net income: add back depreciation and apply every change with the opposite sign for assets and the same sign for liabilities: 63,000 + 21,000 − 15,000 − 3,000 − 12,000 − 5,000 + 1,500 − 600 − 500 + 2,000 = 51,400.

scenes.head: The direct method from two balance sheets

segs.say: Net cash from operating activities is $51,400, by both routes.

Coldharbour’s operating cash flow is $11,600 below its net income, and $32,600 below net income plus depreciation ($84,000 − $51,400): working capital absorbed that cash as Coldharbour let customers owe more, stocked more tile and paid its suppliers down. The second route is the indirect method, which the next lesson develops.

chapters.title: Example: Did Lantern’s first year pay for itself?

scenes.head: Did Lantern’s first year pay for itself?

segs.say: Ana wants to know whether Lantern’s operations funded the year’s investment, and whether the cash commitments that start in 2027 look manageable. Use Lantern’s statement of cash flows above and its noncash note. In 2027 Lantern must pay the first $5,000 instalment on the van note with a year’s interest at 6%, and Coastline’s interest of $150 a quarter.

scenes.head: Did Lantern’s first year pay for itself?

segs.say: Step 1. Operations against investment: 39,940 − 22,000 = 17,940. Operating cash covered the equipment and the van’s down payment with $17,940 to spare.
Step 2. After the dividends: 17,940 − 5,000 = 12,940 was generated internally. The rest of the $42,940 is the $30,000 of stock and borrowing: 12,940 + 30,000 = 42,940.
Step 3. The noncash note reveals a commitment the cash lines don’t show. In 2027: instalment 5,000, van interest 20,000 × 0.06 = 1,200, Coastline interest 4 × 150 = 600; together 6,800.

Step 4. Part of the operating cash is timing. At 31 December Lantern owed $21,289 of operating liabilities that 2027 will settle (bills $9,210, wages $2,100, interest $750, income tax $3,129, and $6,100 of goods and services already paid for), while $13,536 sat in receivables, inventory, supplies and prepaid insurance still to turn into cash or expense. Net, about 21,289 − 13,536 = 7,753 of the operating cash flow is timing that reverses in 2027.

scenes.head: Did Lantern’s first year pay for itself?

segs.say: Yes: operations funded the year’s $22,000 of investing outflows and the $5,000 of dividends, leaving $12,940 of internally generated cash. The 2027 debt payments of about $6,800 look small beside a ten-month operating cash flow of $39,940, but about $7,753 of it is net timing that reverses in 2027.

The statement answers the loan officer’s first question (where the cash came from) directly, and the noncash note answers half of the second (what is owed). The rest needs judgement: a first year’s operating cash flow is flattered, on balance, by unpaid bills and receipts in advance, which the indirect method in the next lesson measures line by line.

scenes.head: From accrual figures to cash: customers and inventory

segs.say: Start from Lantern’s revenue and cost of goods sold, then change the balance sheet movements. Watch which way each change moves the cash figure, and notice that cash collected can exceed revenue when receivables fall or deposits rise. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Interest and dividends under US GAAP and IFRS

segs.say: The same cash flows under three sets of rules. Change the interest and dividends and see how far operating cash flow moves while the total change in cash stays the same. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: “Buying a three-month Treasury bill is an investing outflow.”

segs.say: “Buying a three-month Treasury bill is an investing outflow.”. An investment with a maturity of three months or less when acquired is a cash equivalent, part of the pool the statement explains. Buying it with cash moves money within the pool, so it is not reported as a cash flow (ASC 230-10-45-5). A nine-month certificate of deposit is not a cash equivalent, and buying it is an investing outflow.

scenes.head: “Interest paid is financing, because the loan is financing.”

segs.say: “Interest paid is financing, because the loan is financing.”. Under US GAAP interest paid is operating (ASC 230-10-45-17(d)); only the principal repaid is financing. Under IAS 7 interest paid may currently be operating or financing, and from 2027 most IFRS reporters must show it as financing. Always check which rules a statement follows before comparing operating cash flows.

scenes.head: “The van cost $30,000, so investing outflows include $30,000.”

segs.say: “The van cost $30,000, so investing outflows include $30,000.”. Only the cash paid, $10,000, is an investing outflow. The $20,000 note brought in no cash and paid out none, so it is disclosed as a noncash investing and financing activity (ASC 230-10-50-5). When Lantern repays the principal, those payments will be financing outflows.

scenes.head: “Cash received from customers equals revenue.”

segs.say: “Cash received from customers equals revenue.”. Revenue is earned, not received. Subtract the increase in receivables and any write-offs, and add the increase in unearned revenue. Lantern earned $193,320 and received $191,220; a business whose receivables are falling can receive more than it earns.

scenes.head: “Customer deposits are financing, because the customer is funding us.”

segs.say: “Customer deposits are financing, because the customer is funding us.”. Deposits are receipts from customers for goods or services, so they are operating cash flows when received, even though the revenue is recognised later. Lantern’s $4,040 of catering deposits are inside its $191,220 of cash received from customers.

scenes.head: “If we use the direct method, we don’t need a reconciliation.”

segs.say: “If we use the direct method, we don’t need a reconciliation.”. Under US GAAP a company that uses the direct method must also reconcile net income to net cash from operating activities, in a separate schedule (ASC 230-10-45-30). Under IAS 7 the reconciliation is required only with the indirect method.

scenes.head: Preparing the statement.

segs.say: Preparing the statement. Lantern’s accountant builds the statement two ways and makes them agree. The first route codes the year’s bank transactions by type: receipts from customers, payments to suppliers and staff, interest, tax, equipment, loans, stock and dividends. The second derives the same operating lines from the income statement and the changes in the balance sheet, as in the table above. If the routes disagree, something has been misclassified or missed, often a payment coded to the wrong supplier or a balance sheet account left out of the conversion. The accountant then adds the noncash note for the van and a sentence of policy: Lantern has no cash equivalents.

scenes.head: Comparing borrowers.

segs.say: Comparing borrowers. Coastline Bank’s credit analyst is also reviewing Pellow Roasters, a fictional roaster that reports under IFRS and applies IFRS 18 from 2027. Pellow’s 2027 statement shows net cash from operating activities of $61,000, with interest paid of $8,000 in financing and interest received of $1,500 in investing. To compare it with US GAAP borrowers like Lantern, the analyst moves both back into operating activities: 61,000 − 8,000 + 1,500 = 54,500. On a like-for-like basis Pellow’s operating cash flow is $6,500 lower than reported, and that is the figure the analyst compares with its debt payments.

scenes.head: Reading any statement.

segs.say: Reading any statement. Whatever the framework, the analyst runs the same checks: the closing cash agrees with the balance sheet; the noncash note is read with the investing section, because an asset bought with a note is still an investment and the note is still a debt; the cash-equivalents policy shows what “cash” includes; and the classification of interest and dividends is noted before operating cash flows are compared. Measures built from the statement, such as free cash flow and cash-based coverage ratios, are the subject of F03.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: The statement of cash flows explains the change in cash and cash equivalents over a period by activity: Lantern went from $0 to $42,940 with operating $39,940, investing ($22,000) and financing $25,000.
Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments, generally with a maturity of three months or less when acquired; moving money between cash and cash equivalents is not a cash flow.

Under US GAAP interest paid and received and dividends received are operating, and dividends paid are financing. IAS 7 allows choices until IFRS 18 (from 1 January 2027) makes dividends paid financing for every company and, for most companies, interest paid financing and interest and dividends received investing.

Direct-method lines come from the accrual figures adjusted for the related balance sheet changes: cash collected = revenue − Δreceivables − write-offs + Δunearned revenue; cash paid = expense + Δprepaid or Δinventory − Δpayable.

Noncash investing and financing transactions are left out of the statement and disclosed; only the cash part of a part-cash purchase is included, so Lantern’s van shows $10,000 in investing and a $20,000 note in the disclosure.
ASC 230 and IAS 7 encourage the direct method, but most companies use the indirect method; under US GAAP a company using the direct method must also present the reconciliation of net income.
